segments.text: Section 2. You will listen to a talk about managing your life as a student.
First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Now, listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
Good afternoon, first years.
To continue our series about how to manage your life as a student,
this afternoon I'll give you some advice on how to manage your money.
one of the biggest challenges a student like you will encounter.
The first question is, what costs do you need to consider?
Well, first up, rent and essential bills.
These are all-inclusive in most student halls, as well as some student houses.
But otherwise, you and your housemates will need to organize payments for
for broadband, gas and electricity, water, streaming services and a TV licence if you
want to watch the BBC and football.
To give you an idea of cost, the student's union reckons the typical student will pay
around £70 a month for their essential bills, though you might pay less by going without
a TV or streaming service and by using less water and energy, for example. Taking showers
instead of baths is one example of how you can save money.
And don't forget your personal bills like mobile contracts and subscriptions. It's important
to remember all of your outgoings. You may also have travel and course expenses on top
of your day-to-day costs. Plus, I strongly recommend Student Insurance for things like
laptops as well as antivirus software and a hard drive to back up your work. The handy
Student Finance Calculator at www.gov.uk can help you to work out the financial support
you could get. Two loans are available to full-time students. One to cover the tuition
fees of up to £9,250 and a maintenance loan towards living expenses of up to £9,500 if
you live away from home and also there's £8,000 if you live with your parents.
Student packages do differ in Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland however. If you're going
to manage to live on student loans, plus any grants and money from your parents, you'll
need to budget. Try using an online student budget calculator such as those offered by
UCAS at www.ucas.ac.uk. Then consider these tips. When going out partying, take only the
To set amount of cash you're happy to spend and no plastic cards.
Flash your student card to get all the discounts you can.
If a discount isn't offered, just ask for one.
Secondly, before you buy anything, ask yourself, do I really need it?
Can I afford it?
Is this the cheapest price?
If any one answer is no, don't buy it.
Check out the best value contract and pay as you go mobile for students at specialist
websites such as www.mobilephonesforstudents.co.uk and also www.studentphones.co.uk.
And don't forget, sign up to Skype at www.Skype.com for free calls from your PC.
Before you listen to the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16-20.
Now, listen carefully and answer questions 16-20.
The next thing to consider is to open a bank account.
The banks are all out to lure you with perks on their student accounts, but don't be swayed
by useless gimmicks.
The size of interest-free overdrafts on offer should be the deciding factor when choosing
an account.
Most allow you to go overdrawn for free up to an agreed limit.
When it comes to freebies, only go for those you'll really use.
You need a TV license to watch or record programs as they're being shown on TV, whether you
use a laptop, mobile phone or any other device.
A license covering communal areas and halls of residence won't cover your room.
If you live in a private shared house, you only need one license between everybody unless
you have a separate tenancy agreement for your room, in which case you need your own.
But you don't need a licence at all if you only watch downloaded or streamed TV after
it's been broadcast using websites such as YouTube and on-demand internet services such
as 4OD.
You can apply for a refund if your licence is still valid for at least three whole months
and you no longer need it.
If you work for an employer during term time, you'll pay income tax on any earnings over
your personal allowance.
You'll also pay National Insurance Contributions, NICs, if you earn over £120 a week.
Both are deducted from your wages under the Pay As You Earn, P-A-Y-E, system.
If you're a full-time student and only work in the holidays and your total income for
the year is below the personal allowance, you won't need to pay tax through PAYE if
you fill out form P38S.
Ask an employer for one or download it at www.hmrc.gov.uk.
If you think you've paid too much tax, use the student tax checker online at the same
website.
You now have 30 seconds to check your answers for Section 2.
That is the end of Section 2.
Now turn to Section 3.
